clue.text: Area outside Sunderland essentially writers chose for adaptation

indicators.note: one piece sits outside the other, wrapping around it on both sides
adapting a work reshapes it, so these letters are rearranged into a new form

parts.note: twelve letters of fodder to be rearranged

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central pair of letters is taken

parts.note: the two central letters of the ten-letter city name

explanation.surface: A literary adaptation set in the northeast, with writers picking the region around Sunderland as their backdrop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' works on the rearranged letters, which wrap the middle pair from Sunderland. Sunderland is a city in northeast England, nowhere near this Midlands county.
explanation.definitionFit: Worcestershire is an English county, a region or district of the country, so it is an example of an area.

clue.text: Oasis sound inspires extremely adept English band

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one piece takes others inside it
a word said out loud may be spelt quite differently from how it is heard

parts.note: sound as an adjective means intact or entire, a synonym heard as a hollow

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the word
standard abbreviation
a band worn on the finger

explanation.surface: A music review: some English group with a particular sound, perhaps inspired by the Britpop band Oasis.
explanation.walkthrough: Oasis looks like the Britpop band beside 'English band', but it is the definition. The homophone word is split open after its first letter to take the other three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A watering hole is a pool where animals drink, and an oasis is a fertile spot with water in the desert, so they are near synonyms.

clue.text: Polish pin-up reaches point where comeback's impossible?

parts.note: to polish something is to rub it
an idol or pin-up figure

explanation.surface: A Polish poster girl hitting the point of no return, perhaps in her career.
explanation.walkthrough: Polish, capitalised as the first word, suggests the nationality; it is the verb to shine. The river Rubicon was crossed by Julius Caesar, an irreversible step.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossing the Rubicon is an idiom for taking an irrevocable step, so the river stands for a line beyond which there is no going back.

clue.text: Catch and share new disease ultimately going around

indicators.note: turning around means facing the other way, so the string runs backwards

parts.note: a share is a portion or part
standard abbreviation

indicators.note: what comes ultimately is what comes at the end, so only the last letter counts

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A warning that a new disease is circulating and people catch and share it.
explanation.walkthrough: PART + N + E reads backwards as ENTRAP.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch someone is to trap or ensnare them, so entrap is a straightforward synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Admitting opinion briefly

indicators.note: something said briefly is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a synonym for view or idea, missing its last letter T

explanation.walkthrough: THOUGHT, an opinion, cut short gives THOUGH.
explanation.definitionFit: Though introduces a concession, as in 'granted that', so it works like admitting at the head of a clause.

clue.text: Run cables across Spain, they may need testing?

indicators.note: stretching across something means spanning it, so one piece lies over and around another

parts.note: cricket scoring abbreviation
international vehicle code for Spain (España)
flex is the British word for an electrical cable

explanation.surface: An electrician running wires across Spain, with the equipment needing a safety test afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: R and FLEXES together span E, which falls between them. A flex is the flexible cable on a British appliance.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctors check involuntary responses such as the knee jerk by tapping with a hammer, so these are things that get tested.

clue.text: Deceive Robin maybe over short period of time

indicators.note: in a down entry the piece written over another comes first

parts.note: Robin Hood, the outlaw of Sherwood Forest
as in 'in a wink', an instant

explanation.surface: Tricking a robin, perhaps a bird distracted for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: Robin looks like the bird, but 'maybe' marks it as an example: Robin Hood.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoodwink is to trick or dupe someone, so it is a direct synonym of the verb deceive.

clue.text: Old soldier — or cadet being trained?

indicators.note: training moulds a recruit into a new shape, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: seven letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A veteran compared with a young cadet still going through military training.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash suggests two ways of describing a soldier, veteran or trainee; the whole wordplay is just the two words rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Redcoat was the name for a British soldier of past centuries, from the scarlet tunics of the uniform.

clue.text: Home for llamas, one large enough?

definitions.text: Home for llamas, one large enough?

parts.note: surface reading: the woolly pack animals of the Andes and where they live
setter's reading: only one letter L is needed, turning the animals into Buddhist monks

explanation.surface: Looking for a place roomy enough to house a herd of llamas.
explanation.walkthrough: Large abbreviates to L, and one L is enough: drop the second and llamas become lamas, the monks of Tibetan Buddhism.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan region is the traditional seat of Buddhist lamas, headed by the Dalai Lama, so it is their homeland.

clue.text: A lot not working originally in dumps

indicators.note: what comes originally comes first, so this piece leads the answer

parts.note: as a machine switched off
informal for a great many

explanation.surface: A lot of people out of work and down in the dumps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the dumps' reads as feeling low, but dumps is the verb, and 'originally' moves the second phrase's letters to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To offload something is to get rid of it or unload it, the same as dumping it, both verbs in the third person.

clue.text: Handout with instruction how to undo seat belt?

definitions.text: instruction how to undo seat belt?
definitions.meaning: read literally: push the button marked Release on the buckle

explanation.surface: A leaflet explaining how to unbuckle a car or aircraft seat belt.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase into a command: press the release button. The question mark flags this playful literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A press release is an official statement handed out to journalists, so it is a kind of handout.

clue.text: Figure outspoken detective denied having point of view

indicators.note: what is denied is refused entry, so those letters are taken out of the word

parts.note: outspoken is DIRECT; the detective is DI, a Detective Inspector, removed from it
the angle you take on a story

explanation.surface: A blunt-talking police detective turned down for having an opinion of their own.
explanation.walkthrough: DI is the usual crossword detective (Detective Inspector); taking it out of DIRECT leaves RECT.
explanation.definitionFit: A rectangle is a four-sided geometric shape, and a figure in geometry is any such shape.

clue.text: Women's shocked expression seeing one proceeding to court

parts.note: standard abbreviation for women, as on a clothing size
a comic British exclamation of surprise or alarm

explanation.surface: A woman gasping as she sees someone heading into a courtroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proceeding to court' suggests a lawsuit; the court here is courtship. Ooer is a jokey British exclamation of mock alarm.
explanation.definitionFit: To court someone is to pursue them romantically, and a person who woos or pays suit is doing exactly that.

clue.text: Square, partly Georgian, in Edinburgh

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, so the letters sit inside consecutive words

parts.note: the letters straddle the last word ending and the next two words

explanation.surface: A Georgian square in Edinburgh's New Town, built in part in that period's style.
explanation.walkthrough: Square suggests a town square, backed up by the Georgian architecture of Edinburgh; it is a number. The letters run across georgiaN IN Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: Nine is three multiplied by itself, making it a perfect square number in arithmetic.

clue.text: Worried by element beginning to spoon-feed newborn babies

indicators.note: one piece placed by another stands right next to it

parts.note: the noble gas used in bright signs
as in 'what's eating you?', past tense

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A worried parent learning to spoon-feed new babies.
explanation.walkthrough: Worried reads as anxious; it is the verb in 'eaten up with worry', so ate. The hyphenated word supplies only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Neonate is the medical term for an infant in its first weeks of life, so the plural means newborns.

clue.text: Get involved in heartless attack

indicators.note: without a heart means without its centre, so the middle letter goes

parts.note: to take apart is to criticise savagely; the central A of those nine letters is dropped

explanation.surface: Joining in a callous, cruel assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get involved in' reads as the definition, and 'in' does belong to the idiom, but the setter uses it as the link. Taking apart an argument or a person is to demolish them.
explanation.definitionFit: To take part is to participate or join in an activity, the same idea as becoming involved.

clue.text: Love oddly ignored society set up in county

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: the English county in the southwest

indicators.note: in a down entry, set up means raised, so the letters read bottom to top
ignoring the odd-numbered positions keeps only the even ones

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A county social scene where love is strangely overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: Oddly looks like 'strangely', but it picks letters: ignore the odd positions and keep the even ones. The county is split before its last letter to take them.
explanation.definitionFit: Devotion is deep attachment or loyal affection for a person, which is a kind of love.

clue.text: Suspect that rower almost is creating trouble

indicators.note: almost all of something is short of the whole, so the last letter is cut
something suspect is dodgy or not right, so these letters are out of order

parts.note: used as it stands
the word minus its final R

explanation.surface: A rowing crew suspecting one of its oarsmen of causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Suspect, at the front, looks like the verb; it is the adjective 'dodgy'. Eight letters, THAT plus ROWE, are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in hot water is an idiom for being in a difficult situation or disgrace, so it means trouble.

clue.text: Old Labour promotional film Virginia plugs

indicators.note: a plug is pushed into a gap, so one piece fills the inside of another

parts.note: short for trailer, a preview advertising a film
US state abbreviation

explanation.surface: A political advert for the pre-Blair Labour Party, placed in the state of Virginia.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Labour is the pre-1990s British Labour Party, but here old marks an archaic word for toil, and Labour's capital is only disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Travail is a dated word for hard work or painful effort, and also childbirth, so it is labour in an old usage.

clue.text: Fine food by the sound of it

indicators.note: judging by what is heard, not what is written, points to a spoken likeness

parts.note: fare is the food served at a meal

explanation.surface: Praising some good cooking as it sounds on the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: Fine food suggests gourmet cooking; Fine is the definition on its own, as in fine weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair weather is fine weather, dry and bright, and fair also means acceptable or all right, as fine does.

clue.text: Forsake reckless behaviour

definitions.meaning: verb: to desert or leave behind
noun: a complete lack of restraint, as when people dance wildly

explanation.surface: Advice to give up wild living.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a verb and the second a noun, sharing one spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means desert or give up; as a noun it means uninhibited, carefree lack of restraint.

clue.text: Burn flag after deposing European king

indicators.note: a deposed ruler is removed from power, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: a streamer is a long narrow flag or pennant
E for European, R for Rex, the king; both are removed from the end

explanation.surface: Protesters burning a flag after overthrowing a European monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Burn looks like setting fire to the flag; in Scotland and northern England a burn is a small stream. STREAMER loses its closing E and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A burn is the Scottish word for a brook or small river, so it is a regional name for a running watercourse.

clue.text: Foreign correspondent very severe about Portugal

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: as in penal taxes, punishingly harsh
international vehicle code

explanation.surface: An overseas news reporter being very harsh about Portugal.
explanation.walkthrough: Foreign correspondent suggests a journalist posted abroad, but it is a letter-writing friend in another country. P sits inside PENAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen pal is a friend you exchange letters with, often someone living abroad, so a correspondent from another country.

clue.text: Barely grateful for rent

indicators.note: something laid bare is stripped of its covering, so the outer letters go

parts.note: PLEASED, pleased or thankful, without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A tenant only just thankful for being let a place.
explanation.walkthrough: Barely reads as 'hardly'; here it strips the word bare, removing P and D.
explanation.definitionFit: To lease a property is to let or hire it out for payment, so it matches the verb to rent.

clue.text: Alert when showing dribbling skills, perhaps …

definitions.meaning: idiom for sharp and quick to react
literally: a footballer dribbling has the ball at their feet

explanation.surface: A sharp-witted footballer showing off close control, continued into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on to 25 across, where Arsenal, the London football club, keeps up the football picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the ball is an idiom for being quick-witted and aware, and literally describes a player in possession.

clue.text: .. Arsenal develop amazing energy

indicators.note: to develop something is to change it into a new form, so the letters are rebuilt

parts.note: seven letters of fodder
the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: Arsenal, the London football club, developing an amazing burst of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: After the previous clue, Arsenal reads as the football club; it is a store of weapons. Its capital hides the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A magazine is a storehouse for ammunition and explosives, and an arsenal is likewise a store of weapons.

clue.text: Stages of auxiliary work in retirement

indicators.note: retiring is withdrawing or going back, so the string is read backwards

parts.note: a helper or support
short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: The phases of a retired person's part-time or helping work.
explanation.walkthrough: Stages reads as phases; it is the plural noun for platforms. OP is short for opus.
explanation.definitionFit: Podia is the plural of podium, a raised platform for a speaker or conductor, so it matches stages.

clue.text: Marilyn Monroe was one from album Alan regularly pointed out

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in place, so these letters must be rearranged

parts.note: used as it stands

indicators.note: doing something at regular intervals means every other time, so alternate letters are kept

parts.note: second and fourth letters
used as it stands

explanation.surface: A man called Alan showing someone a picture of Marilyn Monroe in a photo album.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointed out' reads as a single verb; it splits into fodder and the indicator. Album is fodder too, not a clue to a record, so all fourteen letters are in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Monroe's signature hair was a very pale silvery shade, and a woman with hair of that colour is described by this phrase.
